### What the spec proposes

A bookmarks app built around four prioritized user journeys:

| Priority | User story | In the MVP? |
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| **P1** | Save a bookmark (address + optional title) | ✅ core |
| **P1** | Browse the collection and open a bookmark | ✅ core |
| **P2** | Edit and delete bookmarks | management |
| **P3** | Search by keyword and organize with tags | at scale |

It covers **14 functional requirements**, edge cases (invalid addresses, duplicates, empty state, large collections), and **6 measurable success criteria** (e.g. save a bookmark in under 15s, find one in a 500+ collection in under 10s, zero data loss across restarts).

**Key scope boundaries I assumed** (documented in the spec): single user / single device, no accounts or sync, web addresses only, opens in the default browser, and no favicons/previews/import-export in v1.

### Checklist result

Everything passes **except one deliberate open question** I've left for you rather than silently deciding, because it changes scope the most:

> **Question — Who uses this, and where does it run?**
>
> Is this a **single-user app on one device** (personal desktop / mobile / CLI tool), or a **multi-user web service with accounts and sign-in**?
>
> | Option | Answer | Implication |
> |--------|--------|-------------|
> | **A** | Single-user, single device, no accounts *(my default)* | Simplest; no auth, no sync — smallest scope |
> | **B** | Single-user but syncs across my devices | Adds sync/storage-in-the-cloud concerns |
> | **C** | Multi-user web service with sign-in | Adds authentication, per-user isolation — largest scope |
> | **Custom** | Something else | Tell me |

---

**Two things I'd like from you before we move on:**

1. **Answer the scope question above** (or confirm Option A is fine).
2. **Review the spec** — anything to add, cut, or change? Priorities look right? (For example: do you actually want tags/search in v1, or should that wait?)

Once you're happy with the spec, the next gate is **speckit-plan**. I won't plan or write any code until you approve.

Option A is right — this is just for me, on my own device. No sign-in, no accounts. I don't need it syncing across devices either, so let's keep it as simple as that.

The spec is a solid start and the four journeys are basically how I'd use it. A few things jumped out when I pictured actually using it, though:

**Saving should do more of the work for me.** Right now it looks like I type the title in myself. What I'd really expect is: I paste a link, and the app goes and grabs the page's name and a short description on its own, so my list isn't just a wall of raw web addresses. I'd still want to tweak that text if it's wrong — before or after saving — but I shouldn't have to write it from scratch. The little icon for each site (the favicon) would help me scan the list too. So the "no metadata in v1" line — I'd actually want that pulled *into* v1; to me that's part of what makes saving feel finished.

**The duplicate behavior isn't quite what I want.** If I try to save a link I've already got, I don't want to be asked whether to "save anyway" — that just lets me make a mess. I'd rather it quietly take me to the one I already saved so I can update it. No second copy, ever.

**Keep search and tags in from the start — they're not a "someday" thing.** I'm going to pile up a lot of links, so finding them matters early. And when I search, I'd expect it to look *inside* everything — the title, the description, my own notes, the address — not just titles. It shouldn't care about capital letters either. Being able to click a tag to see just those is a must too.

A few smaller things I'd want, which I didn't see:

- **My own notes on a link** — a spot to jot why I saved it, that I can read back later.
- **A way to set a link aside without deleting it forever** — like tucking it out of my main list but keeping it if I want it back. Deleting should stay permanent, but I want a gentler option too.
- **Marking things "read later"** and being able to look at just those unread ones.
- **Choosing how the list is sorted** — newest first, by title, that kind of thing.

Everything else — the empty state, the "no results" message, guarding against accidental deletes — sounds exactly right. Can you fold these in before we plan?

---

## Revised spec ready for review — Gate 1

**Spec file**: `specs/001-manage-bookmarks/spec.md`

### Folded in as committed v1 scope

| Your ask | Now in the spec |
|----------|-----------------|
| **Batch actions** | New **User Story 5** + FR-020/021/022: tick several (or **act on everything currently shown** after a search/filter) and tag / mark read-unread / archive / delete them together. Batch delete keeps the confirmation guard. |
| **Tag suggestions** | FR-019: as you type a tag, the app suggests existing ones so you don't spawn "recipe / recipes / cooking" duplicates. |
| **Precise search** | FR-017 (**quoted = exact phrase**) and FR-018 (**combine a keyword with one or two tags**, including "either tag"). Kept deliberately simple — word + a tag or two, nothing more elaborate. |
| **Import / export** | New **User Story 6** + FR-023–026: import a standard browser bookmarks file on setup (dedup via the one-per-address rule, progress + added/skipped summary, stays responsive on large files); export the whole collection to a portable, re-importable file. |

Read-later/sorting moved to User Story 7 (unchanged in substance).

### On #5 — keeping a copy of the page: you're right, it's bigger

I've parked this in a **"Deferred / Under Discussion"** section rather than committing it, because it's a different *kind* of thing from the rest. Everything else here manages a small bit of text and a link per bookmark. Snapshotting means the app becomes responsible for **capturing and storing whole web pages** — and that opens a cluster of hard questions:

- **How faithful?** Just the readable article text is manageable. A pixel-faithful copy (images, styling, layout) means downloading and rewriting all of a page's assets — a substantial subsystem on its own.
- **Modern pages fight back.** Lots of pages need to run code to render, or sit behind logins/paywalls/cookie walls — snapshots of those range from imperfect to impossible.
- **Storage grows fast.** Full-page copies can be megabytes each; a few thousand bookmarks turns a tiny text database into gigabytes on your disk.
- **It needs its own viewer** to read snapshots back offline.

So realistically it's comparable in effort to a good chunk of the rest of v1 combined. Three ways I'd frame the choice:

| Option | What you get | Rough cost |
|--------|-------------|-----------|
| **A — Defer to v2** | Ship everything above first; add snapshots as a follow-up feature once the core is solid | None now; keeps v1 focused |
| **B — Lightweight "reader" capture in v1** | Save the **article's readable text** (like a reader-mode copy) at save time, viewable offline. Not pixel-faithful, but covers "the page vanished and I want to read what I saved" for most articles | Moderate — a meaningful but bounded addition |
| **C — Full-fidelity snapshot in v1** | A faithful copy of the whole page | Large — biggest single piece of v1; will stretch the timeline noticeably |

My recommendation: **Option B** if reading-back-the-content is the real goal, or **Option A** if you'd rather ship the core fast and add it deliberately later. I'd steer away from C for v1 unless faithful visual copies specifically matter to you.

Let me walk you through it in plain terms — no jargon.

### What kind of app this is

**An app you install on your computer and open like any other app** — works on Mac, Windows, or Linux. Everything lives **on your own machine**: nothing is uploaded anywhere, there's no login, and it works offline. That's the most faithful match to what you asked for (just you, your device, no accounts, no sync).

*Why not a website?* A website would mean a server, an account, and your data living somewhere else — the opposite of what you wanted. An installed app keeps it all private and local.

### How your stuff is stored

Two things sit in a private folder on your computer:
- **A small database** — the fast, searchable index of your bookmarks, tags, notes, and saved searches.
- **A "saved copies" folder** — the actual readable article copies and PDF files.

Keeping the big saved pages as ordinary files (rather than stuffing them into the database) keeps everything fast and easy to back up.

### The part you cared about most — saved copies

When you save a bookmark, the app immediately, **in the background**:
1. Fetches the page's **title, description, and site icon** and fills them in for you.
2. Takes your **readable copy** — the article's text, cleaned up like a "reader mode" — and stores it as a file you can open **even with no internet, even if the original page is gone**.
3. If what you saved is a **PDF**, it keeps **the actual PDF** instead.
4. If it genuinely can't grab a copy (e.g. a page that demands a login), it still saves the bookmark and tells you no copy was captured.

All of that happens **the moment you save**, so the copy is frozen in time — exactly the "the page died but I kept what mattered" behavior you wanted. And it runs in the background so the app never freezes while it works.

### Everything else, briefly

- **Search** is handled by the database's built-in search, so it stays instant even with thousands of bookmarks — case-insensitive, exact phrases in quotes, and word-plus-tag combinations, plus your named **saved searches** (which always re-check against your current bookmarks).
- **Notes** are kept with their formatting (bold, lists, links) intact.
- **Import/export** uses the standard bookmarks file every browser can produce/read — so your existing browser bookmarks come straight in (with an added/skipped summary), and you can always export back out.

**✂️ Long-title tidying (T064).** Titles and descriptions now wrap-and-clamp (even a giant unbroken string), so no monster title can blow out the layout. The reader/edit panel title is guarded too.

**🛟 Error handling (T063).** The two disk-reads now fail soft: a missing saved-copy file shows "no saved copy" instead of erroring, and an unreadable import file reports a zero-summary instead of crashing.

**✅ End-to-end scaffold (T066).** A Playwright smoke test (launch → save → see it in the list) plus its config. Honest caveat: it needs a display, so I could not execute it in this sandbox — it's there for you to run with `npm run test:e2e` on your machine.
